title: Orange with brown or black areas inside: when to throw it away

seo.title: Orange with brown or black areas inside: when to throw it away
seo.meta_description: An orange can hide brown or black tissue. Learn what may cause internal darkening and why moisture, softness, odor, mold and extent matter when deciding to discard it.
seo.search_intent: Orange with brown or black areas inside: when to throw it away

excerpt: Dark internal areas can come from bruising, chilling injury or decay. If the tissue is soft, wet, off-smelling, moldy or extensive, discard the orange.
content_html:
Brown or black areas inside an orange deserve more caution than flesh that is merely dry. Darkening can follow bruising or chilling injury, but it can also represent decay that has advanced from the stem end, a wound, or an internal infection. In a home kitchen, color alone may not reveal the cause. If the area is soft, wet, slimy, off-smelling, moldy, or extensive, discard the entire orange. A tiny dry spot associated with an obvious bruise may be localized damage, but unexplained dark tissue inside a fruit that looked sound outside is a reasonable place to take a conservative approach.

Physical and chilling injury can darken citrus tissue

Oranges can be bruised during harvest, transport, or storage. Mechanical injury breaks cells and can lead to browning just as it does in other fruit. UC Davis also includes brown staining and increased susceptibility to decay among chilling-injury symptoms in oranges. These physiological injuries are not identical to infection, but injured tissue does not retain quality as well.

A dry, firm, sharply limited area near a visible external bruise fits physical injury better than a wet, spreading mass. Even then, you are not required to salvage a fruit if you do not know how long it has been damaged or the darkening extends deeply. A striking internal abnormality is a reasonable reason to throw an orange away.

Several citrus rots can move inward

Citrus fruit is susceptible to a range of postharvest molds and rots. Some begin through rind wounds and others near the stem end. As tissue breaks down, it can become soft, water-soaked, brown or black and develop unusual odors. The outside does not always show the full internal extent at the moment you cut the fruit.

That is why it is unwise to label every black internal patch as harmless “oxidation” and automatically eat adjacent segments. If there is mold, abnormal liquid, collapsing flesh, or a sour, fermented, or rotten smell, treat the orange as spoiled and discard the whole fruit.

Pattern and texture matter more than one shade of brown

Segment membranes and some seeds can naturally appear darker than the juicy flesh, and small color variation is not the same as an invading black lesion. The more concerning change is a localized area that seems to involve the edible tissue, especially when its texture has changed. Compare it with the rest of the orange: wet mushy flesh tells a different story from a thin, light-brown membrane.

Do not taste a clearly deteriorated area simply to decide whether it is safe. Taste is not a food-safety test. When the appearance is uncertain but several abnormal signs occur together, discarding the orange is simpler than trying to identify a specific disease or physiological disorder at home.

Preventing damage also reduces opportunities for decay

When buying oranges, avoid sunken lesions, broken rind, visible mold, and soft leaking areas. Store fruit where it will not be crushed and check neighboring oranges if one begins to decay. Rinse the exterior under running water before cutting even though you do not plan to eat the rind, because the knife passes through the outside before reaching the flesh.

A practical distinction is that pale, dry orange flesh can reflect a physiological quality defect, while brown or black tissue—especially when wet, soft, smelly, or extensive—deserves greater caution. When internal darkening cannot be clearly explained as a tiny, dry bruise, discarding the whole fruit is the safest and simplest choice.

Normal-looking neighboring segments do not rule out an internal focus of decay

Orange segments are divided by membranes, but those membranes do not turn each segment into a sealed safety compartment. Damage or decay beginning near the stem or through the rind can extend internally before every segment changes appearance. If a black area has wet margins or crosses adjacent membranes, the normal color of another segment is not a useful guarantee. Discarding the whole fruit avoids pretending that a home inspection can map the exact boundary of an internal rot.

Use a clean knife and a cutting board that has not just held raw meat when opening citrus. This will not explain a dark spot that was already inside, but it avoids introducing contamination while you inspect the fruit. If you save a sound orange half, refrigerate it covered and use it promptly because cutting removes much of the physical protection provided by the rind.

faq.question: Is a brown area inside an orange normal?
faq.answer: It is not a typical quality feature. It can reflect physical or physiological damage but may also be decay. Wet, soft, extensive, or off-smelling tissue is a reason to discard the fruit.

faq.question: Can I cut out a black part and eat the other orange segments?
faq.answer: If the dark tissue looks like rot or cannot clearly be explained by a tiny dry bruise, the prudent choice is to discard the whole orange rather than salvage segments.
